source_span: the peak in valuation for the S&P coincided with the 10-year yield's breach of 4.50%, the threshold we have long pointed to as the level at which rate sensitivity increases meaningfully for stocks
source_chain: 10-year yield breached 4.50% (back in spring/by May) therefore the S&P's forward multiple compressed to cycle lows therefore mid-teens EPS growth offset that compression, keeping index damage contained and the regime 'classic mid-cycle,' not a breakdown; going forward the swing factor is oil, not the yield level itself ('crude remains the swing factor in the near-term') — another leg higher in crude/product prices is what would push yields/vol up further and the S&P down to a 7000-7100 tactical case, while the 8,000 year-end target stands even in that scenario. Note published Sept 21, before the Sept 23 yield spike, and never references a 5.11% print.
pulse_chain: Hot flash PMI therefore yields spike across the curve and the 10-year closes at 5.11% therefore the desks split on whether this level 'breaks stocks or gets bought' therefore Morgan Stanley, invoking its 4.50% rate-sensitivity threshold and negative stock/yield correlation, takes 'the other side' of JPMorgan's buy-the-dip call — implying the yield level itself is what threatens equities now, with 7000-7100 as the downside if oil climbs further.
why: Morgan Stanley's note (written Sept 21, before the Sept 23 spike, and never mentioning 5.11%) argues the 4.50% breach already happened months ago and earnings growth has since absorbed the damage with an intact bullish 8,000 target, and names oil — not the yield level — as the live forward risk, so casting MS as the bear counterweight arguing 'this yield level breaks stocks' is a mechanism the note does not make.
